analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal sugar price supports, marketing quotas, and taxpayer-funded surplus sugar purchases.
analysis.headline: The SWEETER Act, sponsored by 9 House Republicans, never received a hearing or a vote and died in the House Agriculture Committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the federal sugar program, which guarantees sugar growers and processors a price well above the world market price through government-backed loans, limits on how much sugar can be sold and imported, and a program where the government buys surplus sugar and resells it to bioenergy producers. Those supports are paid for by every household through higher grocery prices and by taxpayers when the government buys surplus sugar. Repealing them would lower sugar prices for food makers and shoppers and end the taxpayer purchases, but would expose a small number of sugar-farming operations to world market prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that buy groceries — sugar is an ingredient in candy, baked goods, cereal, sodas, and many other foods, so the above-market sugar price gets passed into shopping bills. Food and beverage manufacturers would pay closer to world prices for their main sweetener. Taxpayers would also come out ahead, since the bill ends the feedstock flexibility program under which USDA buys surplus sugar from processors to keep them from defaulting on government-backed loans [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Ends the USDA price support loan program that lets sugarcane and sugar beet processors borrow at a guaranteed rate and effectively sets a floor price for domestic sugar well above the world price [S2][S3].

Repeals the sugar marketing allotments and tariff-rate quotas — the quotas on how much sugar domestic processors can sell and how much can be imported at low tariff rates — which are the main tools that keep US sugar prices high [S2][S3].

Eliminates the feedstock flexibility program, under which the USDA purchases surplus sugar from processors and resells it to bioenergy producers to avoid loan forfeitures — spending that comes out of the Treasury when the program's own quotas don't clear the market [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors, concentrated in a handful of states, would lose the guaranteed above-market price and import protection and would have to compete at world sugar prices. Farm towns and processing operations that depend on that premium would bear the adjustment.

drawbacks.text: Sugar growers and processors, who have organized their businesses around guaranteed above-market prices, would take real losses adjusting to world prices, and jobs in sugar-processing regions would be at risk [S2].

The world sugar market is itself distorted by heavy foreign subsidies, so a unilateral repeal would open US producers to competition from governments that subsidize their own sugar industries — the strongest good-faith case supporters of the current program make, and this bill contains no phase-out or transition aid to soften the blow [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are spread thin but broad — a few dollars a year in lower food costs for most households and an end to taxpayer purchases of surplus sugar — while the losses are concentrated and steep for the relatively few sugar-farming and processing operations that depend on the program. That imbalance is exactly why the program survives: the beneficiaries of repeal barely notice it, while the losers fight hard for it. The bill's abrupt full repeal, with no transition, makes the concentrated pain worse than it needed to be, but the underlying case — consumers and taxpayers paying a few thousand sugar producers to keep prices high — favors repeal.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Perry introduced the SWEETER Act on October 22, 2021, with 8 Republican cosponsors signing on the same day [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture on the day it was introduced — the committee with jurisdiction over every farm subsidy program, including sugar [S5].
On November 3, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management. That was the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar growers and processors are better off because the bill died: they keep the guaranteed above-market prices, import limits, and government surplus purchases. Consumers and taxpayers continue paying for the program.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 sponsors were Republicans and the Democratic-controlled Agriculture Committee never took it up, but no vote was ever recorded, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.industry: Sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors
industries.note: The sugar program is the industry's core economic support: it guarantees processors a price well above the world market through loans, caps domestic sales and imports, and has USDA buy surplus sugar when quotas leave processors holding too much. Repeal would end all three, exposing growers to world prices; the industry's gain under the status quo comes directly out of grocery bills and federal spending.

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers (candy, baked goods, cereals, sodas)
industries.note: These companies buy sugar as a major input at prices inflated by the quota and loan programs, and have long pushed for repeal. Cheaper sugar would lower their costs and, competitively, shoppers' prices.

The feedstock flexibility program supplies them with surplus sugar purchased by USDA as a raw material. Repealing it removes that feedstock channel, though it also ends a taxpayer-funded market distortion.
